passages.title: Reading Comprehension I – China’s social programmes
passages.instructions: Read the following text, and answer the questions that follow. For items 1–6, choose the most appropriate answer for each item according to the information in the reading text. For items 7–10, choose the best contextual meaning for each highlighted word in the text.
paragraphs: Over the last few decades, China has registered impressive economic development. Many have indicated to the environmental costs associated with this phenomenal growth. However, there are also social problems that are associated with the transition of the country from agrarian and rural to ultra-modern urban economy. The government has designed a number of programs to tackle these social problems as the following three examples illustrate.

In hope of a better life, millions of young rural labourers have left their hometowns in recent decades to work in cities, leaving old people and children behind in their home villages. Now, China is encouraging migrant workers to return home and start their own businesses amid efforts to encourage rural development and reduce poverty. The government will unveil more policies to support migrant workers who want to start businesses in their hometowns.

The return of skilled and experienced migrant workers can help promote social and economic development in rural areas and ultimately stimulate rural development. Last year, the government released a plan ordering local authorities, commercial banks and financial guarantee firms to expand financial support for returning migrant workers who plan to start businesses.

China had more than 286.5 million migrant workers at the end of 2017. More than 7 million migrant workers have returned to their hometowns to start their own businesses, and each new entrepreneur helps boost local employment by providing an average of four new employment opportunities, according to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security.

On the other hand, China’s Ministry of Civil Affairs has issued a document calling for better social care for left-behind elderly people in rural areas. In an effort to reduce security risks to rural seniors, many of whom live alone while younger family members work in cities, China will establish a database containing information on these left-behind elderly people, the Ministry said.

Authorities will set up a regular visitor program to check on rural left-behind seniors. To improve elderly care in rural areas, the Ministry promised to improve the management of nursing homes and to build more facilities. The Ministry encourages family members to visit elderly relatives more often while urging village committees, charity organizations and volunteers to spend time with them so as to prevent loneliness. The Ministry said that China had more than 144,600 nursing institutions as of September 2017, three times the number at the end of 2012.

Finally, according to the Office of the National Commission on Aging, the number of people aged 60 and above has reached 241 million in China by the end of 2017, accounting for 17.3 percent of the total population. A society with 10 percent of its population aged 60 or older is considered an aging society.

Since China first qualified as an aging society in 1999, the number of people aged 60 or above has seen an overall increase of 110 million. It is estimated that the number of seniors will peak at 487 million around the year 2050, 34.9 percent of the total population. The government has stepped up nationwide education on aging with the aim of raising citizens’ awareness and has called on the public to care for the elderly.
passages.note: Text as printed (including ‘Many have indicated to …’). The highlighted (bold) words in the paper are: phenomenal, unveil, stimulate, risks.

passages.title: Reading Comprehension II – Tracking animals from space (ICARUS)
passages.instructions: Read the following text, and answer the questions that follow. For items 66–75, choose the most appropriate answer for each item according to the information in the reading text. For items 76–80, choose the best contextual meaning for each highlighted word in the text.
paragraphs: A team of scientists from the International Cooperation for Animal Research Using Space, ICARUS, is planning to track animal migration from space, or rather, from the International Space Station, ISS. Normally, migrating birds have numbered rings attached to their feet, for example, so that they can be identified elsewhere at later date and their migratory paths traced back. Nowadays, researchers prefer to attach wireless tracking devices to the birds to trace their paths more accurately. It can now even be done by satellite. So far, however, conventional satellites have only delivered fairly rough information.

ICARUS is supposed to throw this so-called animal telemetry, and thus ecology in general, into a whole new dimension. “Our antenna on the ISS will be able to control far more transmitters concurrently, and much more accurately than has been possible so far,” says one scientist from ICARUS. “And we won’t just collect location data but also data on acceleration, temperature, air pressure, heart rate and anything else we want to measure.” This is all enabled by the tininess of sensor technology. The birds’ trip recorders, known as tags, are currently not much bigger than a finger-tip and only weigh a few grams. Soon, it will even be possible to tag insects.

Each of the tags has a tiny hard disc which records data for an entire lifetime. Scientists will be able to track the birds’ whole life history in minute detail with GPS accuracy: when and where they sleep, feed, fight and why they die. Their aim over time is to see thousands of animals tagged all over the world. Blackbirds in Europe, for example, in order to discover why some head for wintering grounds and others don’t; domestic cats to check to what extent they really endanger the songbird population; whales and sea turtles to find out how they can be better protected. And the animals are supposed to do us humans a service, too. They can be our eyes, ears and noses in places we have little chance of getting to ourselves. They can keep us updated on the state of our planet.

Animals react to pollutants; they quickly reveal an outbreak of avian flu and can register the approach of a devastating swarm of locusts. Indeed, they may even be able to alert us to volcanic eruptions and earthquakes hours before measuring instruments register anything. This is one of the themes scientists are currently investigating by tagging, amongst others, sheep and goats; to date, the animals have always sought shelter roughly five hours before a major eruption – all around the volcano, which means other causes can be excluded. What exactly they sense, we still don’t know, the scientists say. They have a kind of sixth sense. But their movement patterns clearly indicate their escape behaviour.

In other words, tagged animals can provide us humans with a network of highly-intelligent, world-spanning monitoring points and warning devices, and reveal completely new ecological interrelations. Scientist now plan to expand the project and install additional antennas with satellites in space. By making animal observation from space more continuous, the aim is to gain a deeper understanding of the processes in nature. Global institutions like the World Health Organization and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change have already signalled their interest.
passages.note: Text as printed (‘at later date’, ‘Scientist now plan’). Highlighted (bold) words: conventional, supposed, tininess, track, devastating.

questions.stem: What are the social problems the government in China is trying to solve?
explanation_steps: The first paragraph says the government designed programs to tackle social problems ‘as the following three examples illustrate’.

The three examples are: migrant workers (encouraged to return home and start businesses), left-behind elderly people (database, visitor program, nursing homes) and the aging society (education on aging).
All three options are covered. Answer: D.
tips: When a passage announces ‘the following three examples’, count them – each one is usually an option.

similar_questions.stem: A text says a town council is tackling three problems: unemployment, poor roads and a lack of clean water. Which problems is the council trying to solve?
explanation_steps: All three problems are named in the text. Answer: D.

questions.stem: One of the following statements <u>does not</u> represent a benefit of the return of migrant workers to their hometowns and villages as entrepreneurs.

options.A: The return of migrant workers encourages economic development in rural areas.
options.B: The return of migrant workers promotes social development in rural areas.
options.C: The return of migrant workers decreases the problem of aging.
options.D: The return of migrant workers provides employment opportunities to rural communities.

explanation_steps: Stated benefits: ‘help promote social and economic development in rural areas’ (A, B) and ‘each new entrepreneur helps boost local employment by providing an average of four new employment opportunities’ (D).
Nothing in the passage links the returning workers to the aging problem, which is treated as a separate issue. Answer: C.
tips: For a NOT question, tick each option you can find in the text; the one left over is the answer.

similar_questions.stem: A text says new irrigation ‘raises harvests and creates jobs for young people’. Which is NOT a benefit mentioned?
explanation_steps: School fees are never mentioned. Answer: C.

questions.stem: One of the following <u>is not</u> an accurate statistics representing the year 2017.

options.A: There were 286.5 million migrant workers in 2017.
options.B: There were 7 million migrant workers who returned to their hometowns in 2017.
options.C: There were more than 144,600 nursing institutions by September of 2017.
options.D: The number of people aged 60 and above had reached 241 million in 2017.
options.E: The number of people aged 60 and above had reached 487 million in 2017.

explanation_steps: 487 million is the ESTIMATED peak number of seniors ‘around the year 2050’, not a 2017 figure; in 2017 the number was 241 million.
A, C and D repeat 2017 figures from the text. Answer: E.
tips: Numbers in reading questions are often moved to the wrong year – check which year each figure belongs to.

similar_questions.stem: A text says: ‘The town had 20,000 people in 2010; the population is expected to reach 50,000 by 2040.’ Which is NOT accurate for 2010?
explanation_steps: 50,000 is the forecast for 2040. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Keyed E (487 million is the 2050 estimate). Option B is also loosely worded: the text says ‘More than 7 million migrant workers have returned’ (cumulative, no year given), not 7 million in 2017. E is the clearly intended answer – teacher decision whether B should also be accepted.

questions.stem: Which one of the following government institutions <u>is not</u> mentioned in the passage?

options.A: Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security
options.C: Office of the National Commission on Aging

explanation_steps: The passage names the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (paragraph 4), the Ministry of Civil Affairs (paragraph 5) and the Office of the National Commission on Aging (paragraph 7).
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is never mentioned. Answer: D.
tips: Scan for capital letters – names of institutions stand out quickly.

similar_questions.stem: A report quotes the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Education. Which institution is NOT mentioned?
explanation_steps: Only Health and Education are quoted. Answer: C.

questions.stem: To address the problem of left-behind elderly people, the government is promising to do one of the following.

options.A: To set up a regular visitor program to check on rural left-behind seniors.
options.B: To improve the management of nursing homes and build more facilities.
options.C: To encourage volunteers to spend time with left-behind seniors.

explanation_steps: Paragraph 6: ‘Authorities will set up a regular visitor program…’ (A); ‘the Ministry promised to improve the management of nursing homes and to build more facilities’ (B); the Ministry is ‘urging village committees, charity organizations and volunteers to spend time with them’ (C).
All three are stated. Answer: D.
tips: Before choosing ‘All of the above’, confirm every single option in the text.

similar_questions.stem: To reduce traffic accidents the city will add traffic lights, train drivers and lower speed limits. What will the city do?
explanation_steps: All three measures are listed. Answer: D.

questions.stem: The Chinese population is considered an aging society because

options.A: more than 10 percent of the population is aged 60 years and above.
options.B: 34.9 percent of the population is aged 60 years and above.
options.C: the proportion of girls to boys is decreasing.
options.D: the number of migrant workers is increasing.
options.E: the number of left-behind elderly people is increasing.

explanation_steps: Definition in the text: ‘A society with 10 percent of its population aged 60 or older is considered an aging society.’ China has 17.3 percent.
34.9 percent (B) is the 2050 estimate, not the reason. Answer: A.
tips: Look for a definition sentence (‘… is considered …’) – it usually gives the ‘because’.

similar_questions.stem: ‘A country where more than half the people live in towns is called urbanised. In Country X, 62% live in towns.’ Country X is urbanised because

options.A: more than 50% of its people live in towns.

explanation_steps: Apply the definition: over 50% urban. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word: ‘Many have indicated to the environmental costs associated with this phenomenal growth.’ — phenomenal
explanation_steps: The growth is described as ‘impressive’ in the previous sentence, so ‘phenomenal’ means remarkable, extraordinary.
‘Ordinary’, ‘commonplace’ and ‘typical’ are opposites. Answer: D (exceptional).
tips: Use the neighbouring sentence: ‘impressive economic development … this phenomenal growth’ refers to the same thing.

similar_questions.stem: ‘The singer’s first album was a phenomenal success; it sold ten million copies.’ phenomenal means
explanation_steps: Ten million copies = extraordinary. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘phenomenal’ in this context means ‘exceptional, extraordinary’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word: ‘The government will unveil more policies to support migrant workers…’ — unveil
explanation_steps: To unveil (literally ‘remove the veil from’) policies is to make them known publicly for the first time.
uncover, reveal, disclose and publicize all express ‘make known’. Answer: E (All of the above).
tips: When four options are near-synonyms and one is ‘All of the above’, that is usually the key.

similar_questions.stem: ‘The company will unveil its new phone next week.’ unveil means

options.A: present publicly for the first time

explanation_steps: To unveil a product = show it publicly for the first time. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘unveil’ in this context means ‘reveal / make public’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word: ‘…can help promote social and economic development in rural areas and ultimately stimulate rural development.’ — stimulate
explanation_steps: ‘stimulate’ is joined with ‘promote … development’, so it is positive: encourage, boost.
slow down, decrease and discourage are opposites; steal is unrelated. Answer: C.
tips: Words linked by ‘and’ in the same sentence usually have a similar positive or negative sense.

similar_questions.stem: ‘Lower taxes can stimulate business growth.’ stimulate means
explanation_steps: Lower taxes help growth. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘stimulate’ in this context means ‘encourage’.

questions.stem: Choose the best contextual meaning of the highlighted word: ‘In an effort to reduce security risks to rural seniors, many of whom live alone…’ — risks
explanation_steps: Old people living alone face dangers (accidents, crime, illness with nobody to help). The government wants to reduce these ‘risks’.
‘security’ and ‘safety’ are what the government wants to increase; ‘chance’ is too neutral. Answer: B.
tips: Test the option in the sentence: ‘reduce security dangers’ makes sense; ‘reduce security safety’ does not.

similar_questions.stem: ‘Smoking increases the risk of heart disease.’ risk means
explanation_steps: Risk = possibility of something bad. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: ‘risks’ in this context means ‘dangers’.

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate conjunction to fill in the blank space: ‘_____ the student was very sick, she attended her class regularly and did well in her exams.’
explanation_steps: The two ideas contrast (very sick ↔ attended regularly and did well), and the blank is followed by a full clause (the student was very sick).

‘Although’ + clause expresses contrast. ‘Despite’ needs a noun/-ing (Despite being very sick…); ‘But’ cannot begin the subordinate clause here; ‘Because’ and ‘Unless’ give the wrong meaning. Answer: B.
tips: although + subject + verb; despite / in spite of + noun or -ing.

similar_questions.stem: _____ it was raining heavily, the farmers continued working.
explanation_steps: Contrast + full clause → Although. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: although/though + clause; despite/in spite of + noun phrase or -ing.

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate conjunction to fill in the blank space: ‘Alcohol is known to be dangerous to health, ___ many people continue to consume it.’
explanation_steps: The second clause is unexpected given the first (dangerous → people still drink it): a contrast.
‘yet’ (= but, nevertheless) joins two contrasting clauses. ‘so’ = result, ‘because’ = reason, ‘moreover’ = addition, ‘in spite of’ needs a noun. Answer: E.
tips: ‘, yet’ between two clauses means ‘but surprisingly’.

similar_questions.stem: He studied very hard, ___ he failed the test.
explanation_steps: Unexpected result → yet. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.rule: yet joins two clauses with a surprising contrast.

questions.stem:
My brother and I visited three places last month: Shanghai, Paris, and Dubai. Shanghai is very interesting, but for me, Paris is __13__ than Shanghai, and Dubai is __14__ of all because it is so different in some ways. It is the hottest, driest and __15__ of all.
Choose the best option for blank 13.
explanation_steps: ‘than Shanghai’ compares two things → comparative.
Long adjective (interesting) → more interesting. Answer: B.
tips: ‘than’ → comparative (-er / more); ‘of all’ / ‘in the class’ → superlative (the -est / the most).

similar_questions.stem: This book is ___ than the one I read last week.
explanation_steps: ‘than’ → comparative. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: more + long adjective + than.

questions.stem:

Choose the best option for blank 14.
explanation_steps: ‘of all’ compares Dubai with all three places → superlative with ‘the’.
Answer: A (the most interesting).
tips: ‘of all’ is a superlative signal.

similar_questions.stem: Of all my subjects, mathematics is ___.
explanation_steps: ‘Of all’ → superlative. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: the most + long adjective (+ of all / in the group).

questions.stem:
My brother and I visited three places last month: Shanghai, Paris, and Dubai. Shanghai is very interesting, but for me, Paris is __13__ than Shanghai, and Dubai is __14__ of all because it is so different in some ways. It is the hottest, driest and __15__ of all.
Choose the best option for blank 15.
explanation_steps: ‘the hottest, driest and ___ of all’: a list of superlatives sharing one ‘the’.
The superlative of modern is ‘(the) most modern’; the ‘the’ before ‘hottest’ covers all three. Answer: C.
tips: In a list of superlatives, ‘the’ is often written only once: the tallest, strongest and most famous.

similar_questions.stem: It is the biggest, cleanest and ___ hotel in the town.
explanation_steps: A list of superlatives → most comfortable. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: the + superlative, superlative and most + adjective.

similar_questions.stem: Farmers should plant more trees than the trees that ___ cut every year.

textbook_ref.topic: Present simple – agreement in relative clauses

Teacher: No, you cannot carry on working alone. You must be tired now. So let’s __28__ digging new holes until Tuesday. How many seedlings did you plant yesterday?

similar_questions.stem: It is raining, so we will ___ the football match until next week.

Teacher: No, you cannot carry on working alone. You must be tired now. So let’s __28__ digging new holes until Tuesday. How many seedlings did you plant yesterday?

similar_questions.stem: We couldn’t finish the painting because we ___ paint.

questions.stem:
Policeman: This is a ‘no parking’ zone. You __30__ park here.

Prohibition → must not. (‘may not’ is weaker/formal permission; ‘will not’ is a prediction.) Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: This is a hospital. You ___ make noise here.

Choose the most appropriate modal verb for blank 31.
explanation_steps: The policeman says the apology is unnecessary: ‘Just move the car.’
No necessity → need not. ‘must not’ would forbid apologizing; ‘had not to’ is not correct English. Answer: A.
tips: need not (needn’t) = it is not necessary.

similar_questions.stem: You ___ bring food; lunch is provided.
explanation_steps: Not necessary → need not. Answer: B.

I + must. ‘has to’ does not agree with ‘I’ (I have to); ‘had to’ is past; might/may express only possibility. Answer: E.
tips: Check subject–verb agreement: I have to / he has to.

similar_questions.stem: I ___ finish this report before I go home tonight.
explanation_steps: Present obligation, subject I → must. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: must / have to for present obligation; he has to, I have to.

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate alternative: ‘One of the teachers ___ for further education to China last year.’
explanation_steps: Subject = ‘One (of the teachers)’ → singular.
‘last year’ → past simple; the teacher was sent by someone → passive: was sent. Answer: A.
tips: ‘One of + plural noun’ takes a singular verb.

similar_questions.stem: One of my friends ___ a prize last week.
explanation_steps: One → singular; last week → past. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Subject–verb agreement: one of + plural noun
textbook_ref.rule: The verb agrees with ‘one’ (singular).

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate alternative: ‘Both my daughter and my son ___ their English exam this time tomorrow.’
explanation_steps: ‘this time tomorrow’ = an action in progress at a point in the future → future continuous.
will be + -ing: will be doing. Answer: C.
tips: this time tomorrow / at 10 o’clock tomorrow → will be + -ing.

similar_questions.stem: This time next week, we ___ on the beach.
explanation_steps: Future continuous. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: will be + -ing for an action in progress at a future time.

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate alternative: ‘The ___ desks of the school are being collected by the storekeeper.’
explanation_steps: The adjective before ‘desks’ must describe desks that have been damaged → past participle used as an adjective (passive meaning).
broken desks. Answer: A.
tips: -ed/-en participle adjective = something done to the noun (broken glass); -ing = the noun does it (a barking dog).

similar_questions.stem: Please throw away the ___ cups.
explanation_steps: Cups that have been cracked. Answer: B.

questions.stem:
Suleman: You look tired. Didn’t you sleep well?
Yonas: No, I didn’t. The ___ dogs disturbed our neighbourhood throughout the night.
explanation_steps: The dogs were doing the action (they barked) → present participle -ing as an adjective.
the barking dogs. Answer: C.
tips: Active meaning → -ing adjective.

similar_questions.stem: We could not sleep because of the ___ baby.
explanation_steps: The baby is crying. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate alternative: ‘There were only ___ female students present in the seminar, because they were not informed in advance.’
explanation_steps: ‘only’ + the reason (not informed) → a small number. ‘students’ is countable plural.
a few (small number, countable). ‘a little’ and ‘much’ are for uncountable nouns; many / a lot of contradict ‘only’. Answer: A.
tips: few / a few / many → countable; little / a little / much → uncountable.

similar_questions.stem: Only ___ people came to the meeting because it was raining.
explanation_steps: Countable, small number. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.topic: Quantifiers: a few / a little / many / much

questions.stem:
Student: Why are you spraying these mango trees with pesticide?
Gardener: I’m spraying pesticide ___ the pests will be killed before they damage the mangoes.
explanation_steps: The second clause gives the PURPOSE of spraying.
Purpose + clause → so that. ‘because’ would give a reason, not an aim. Answer: B.
tips: so that + subject + will/can/could = purpose.

similar_questions.stem: She saved money ___ she could buy a bicycle.
explanation_steps: Purpose. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.topic: Purpose clauses: so that / in order to

questions.stem: Give your agreement to the statement provided: ‘Dogs perform an important function for the blind.’
explanation_steps: The statement is present simple with a main verb (perform) and a plural subject (dogs → they).
Agreement = Yes + they + do. Answer: A.
tips: Short answers repeat the auxiliary: main verb in present simple → do/does.

similar_questions.stem: Agree: ‘Farmers work very hard.’
explanation_steps: Present simple, plural → Yes, they do. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: Yes/No + pronoun + auxiliary of the statement.

questions.stem: Give your disagreement to the statement provided: ‘People are taking care of the environment.’
explanation_steps: The auxiliary in the statement is ‘are’ (present continuous).
Disagreement = No + they + aren’t. Answer: E.
tips: No goes with a negative auxiliary; Yes goes with a positive one.

similar_questions.stem: Disagree: ‘The children are sleeping.’
explanation_steps: No, they aren’t. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: Yes/No + pronoun + auxiliary of the statement.

questions.stem: Choose the logical question for the italicized answer: ‘Because I need it for my job.’

options.A: How often do you have English classes?
options.B: Why are you taking English classes?
options.C: When did you start taking English classes?
options.D: Why is he taking English classes daily?
options.E: Do you need English in your job?

explanation_steps: An answer beginning ‘Because…’ answers a ‘Why’ question.
The answer uses ‘I’, so the question must use ‘you’: Why are you taking English classes? (D asks about ‘he’.) Answer: B.
tips: Match both the question word (Because → Why) and the person (I ↔ you).

similar_questions.stem: Answer: ‘Because I missed the bus.’ Question?
explanation_steps: Because → Why; I → you. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Choose the logical question for the italicized answer: ‘Sorry, I am a stranger here myself.’

options.A: Excuse me. Could you please tell me the way to the Italian embassy?
options.D: Would you please tell me your address?
options.E: How long have you been here?

explanation_steps: ‘I am a stranger here myself’ is the polite way to say ‘I don’t know this area, so I can’t give you directions.’
It answers a request for directions. Answer: A.
tips: Learn fixed replies: ‘Sorry, I’m a stranger here (myself)’ = I can’t help with directions.

similar_questions.stem: Reply: ‘Sorry, I don’t know this area at all.’ Question?

options.A: Could you tell me where the post office is?

explanation_steps: It answers a request for directions. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.topic: Functional language – asking for and giving directions

questions.stem: Choose the correct rewritten form of the italicized sentence: ‘The performance of the team in the second half satisfied the coach.’

options.A: The teams performance in the second half satisfied the coach.
options.B: The teams’ performance in the second half satisfied the coach.
options.C: The team performance in the second half satisfied the coach.
options.D: The team’s performance in the second half satisfied the coach.
options.E: The team of performance in the second half satisfied the coach.

explanation_steps: ‘the performance of the team’ (one team) → possessive ’s on a singular noun: the team’s performance.
‘teams’’ would mean several teams; ‘teams’ has no apostrophe. Answer: D.
tips: Singular owner + ’s; plural owner ending in s + ’ only.

similar_questions.stem: Rewrite: ‘the bag of the teacher’.
explanation_steps: One teacher → teacher’s. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: singular noun + ’s; plural noun in -s + ’.

questions.stem: Choose the inverted form of the given sentence in italics: ‘Teachers no longer give detailed grammar notes to their students.’

options.A: No longer teachers give detailed grammar notes to their students.
options.B: Do no longer teachers give detailed grammar notes to their students.
options.C: No longer do teachers give detailed grammar notes to their students.
options.D: No longer does teachers give detailed grammar notes to their students.
options.E: Teachers do no longer gives detailed grammar notes to their students.

explanation_steps: When a negative adverbial (No longer) begins the sentence, use question word order: No longer + auxiliary + subject + main verb.
Present simple, plural subject → do: No longer do teachers give… (‘does’ does not agree with ‘teachers’). Answer: C.
tips: Inversion: Never / Seldom / No longer / Not only + do/does/did + subject + base verb.

similar_questions.stem: Invert: ‘We rarely see such talent.’

options.B: Rarely do we see such talent.
options.C: Rarely does we see such talent.
options.D: Do rarely we see such talent.
options.E: We do rarely see such talent.

explanation_steps: Rarely + do + we + see. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: No longer / Never / Rarely + auxiliary + subject + verb.

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech form: The director said to the parents, “Do you regularly come and ask the teachers about your children?”

options.A: The director asked the parents if they regularly came and asked the teachers about their children.
options.B: The director asked the parents if they regularly come and ask the teachers about their children.
options.C: The director asked the parents if they are regularly coming and asking the teachers about their children.
options.D: The director asked the parents if they regularly came and asked the teachers about your children.
options.E: The director asked the parents they regularly came and asked the teachers about their children.

explanation_steps: Yes/no question → asked + if/whether + statement word order.
Backshift present simple → past simple: come → came, ask → asked; pronouns change: you → they, your → their.
B keeps the present, D keeps ‘your’, E omits ‘if’. Answer: A.
tips: Reported yes/no question: asked (+ object) + if/whether + subject + verb (no ‘do’).

similar_questions.stem: She said to me, “Do you like football?”

options.A: She asked me if I liked football.
options.B: She asked me if do I like football.
options.C: She asked me if you liked football.
options.D: She asked me I liked football.
options.E: She asked me if I like football?

explanation_steps: if + backshift + pronoun change. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: asked + if/whether + subject + verb (tense backshifted).

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech form: He said to his friends, “I have worked here since I left my first job.”

options.A: He said to his friends that he worked here since he left his first job.
options.B: He said to his friends that I worked here since I left my first job.
options.C: He said to his friends that he had worked there since he had left his first job.
options.D: He said to his friends that I had worked there since I had left my first job.
options.E: He said to his friends that he has worked there since he had left his first job.

explanation_steps: Backshift: have worked → had worked; left → had left. Place: here → there. Pronoun: I → he.
Only C makes all the changes. Answer: C.
tips: here → there, now → then, I → he/she, present perfect → past perfect.

similar_questions.stem: She said, “I have lived here for ten years.”

options.A: She said that she had lived there for ten years.
options.B: She said that I had lived there for ten years.
options.C: She said that she has lived here for ten years.
options.D: She said that she lived here for ten years.
options.E: She said she had lived here for ten years.

explanation_steps: had lived + there + she. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: present perfect → past perfect; past → past perfect; here → there.

questions.stem: Choose the correct direct speech form: ‘My classmate asked me when I was going to go to our school library.’

options.A: “When are we going to our school library?” my classmate asked me.
options.B: “When am I going to our school library?” my classmate asked me.
options.C: “When will we go to our school library?” my classmate asked me.
options.D: “When are you going to go to our school library?” my classmate asked me.
options.E: “When do you go to our school library?” my classmate asked me.

explanation_steps: Reverse the changes: was going to go → are going to go; ‘I’ (the listener) → ‘you’ in the classmate’s words.
Answer: D.
tips: Going back to direct speech: forward-shift the tense and change the pronouns to the speaker’s point of view.

similar_questions.stem: Direct speech: ‘He asked me where I was going to stay.’

options.A: “Where are you going to stay?” he asked me.
options.B: “Where am I going to stay?” he asked me.
options.C: “Where was I going to stay?” he asked me.
options.D: “Where is he going to stay?” he asked.
options.E: “Where were you going to stay?” he asked me.

explanation_steps: was going to → are going to; I → you. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form: ‘The students are revising the previous years’ exam papers these days.’

options.A: The previous years’ exam papers are revising by the students these days.
options.B: The previous years’ exam papers are being revised by the students these days.
options.C: The previous years’ exam papers are revised by the students these days.
options.D: These days, the students were revising the previous years’ exam papers.
options.E: The previous years’ exam papers are being revising by the students these days.

explanation_steps: Active present continuous (are revising) → passive present continuous: are being + past participle (revised).
Answer: B.
tips: Keep the tense: present continuous active → am/is/are being + past participle.

similar_questions.stem: Passive: ‘Workers are building a new school.’

options.A: A new school is built by workers.
options.B: A new school is being built by workers.
options.C: A new school is being building by workers.
options.D: A new school was built by workers.
options.E: A new school builds by workers.

explanation_steps: is being built. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: are revising → are being revised.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form: ‘Can I download all of this information from the Internet tomorrow?’

options.A: I can download all of this information from the Internet tomorrow.
options.B: Could all of this information be downloaded from the Internet tomorrow?
options.C: Can I download all of this information from the Internet tomorrow?
options.D: Can be all of this information downloaded from the Internet tomorrow?
options.E: Can all of this information be downloaded from the Internet tomorrow?

explanation_steps: Modal passive = modal + be + past participle; a question puts the modal first: Can + subject + be + past participle?
Keep ‘can’ (not could). Answer: E.
tips: Passive questions with modals: Can/Will/Should + new subject + be + past participle?

similar_questions.stem: Passive: ‘Can we finish the work today?’

options.A: Can the work be finished today?
options.B: Can be the work finished today?
options.C: Could the work be finished today?
options.D: The work can be finished today.

explanation_steps: Can + subject + be + pp. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.rule: modal + be + past participle; question: modal + subject + be + pp?

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘My mother always reads books and so does my father.’

options.A: Both my mother and my father always read books.
options.B: Only my mother likes reading books.
options.C: My father does not like reading books.
options.E: My mother likes reading and my father likes exercising.

explanation_steps: ‘so does my father’ = my father also always reads books.
Answer: A (Both … read).
tips: so + auxiliary + subject = ‘too’; neither + auxiliary + subject = ‘not either’.

similar_questions.stem: ‘Aman speaks French and so does his sister.’

options.B: Both Aman and his sister speak French.

explanation_steps: so does = also. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘Nobody understands the global issues better than he does.’

options.A: Everybody understands the global issues in different ways.
options.B: He has a better understanding of the global issues than others.
options.C: He understands the global issues as well as everybody else.
options.D: Everybody finds it difficult to understand the global issues.
options.E: He is the only person who understands the global issues.

explanation_steps: ‘Nobody … better than he’ = he understands them best / better than the others.
E goes too far (others may understand them too, just not better). Answer: B.
tips: Negative + comparative (nobody … better than X) = X is the best.

similar_questions.stem: ‘No student in the class runs faster than Lula.’

options.A: Lula runs faster than the others.

explanation_steps: Lula is the fastest. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘Unlike her elder brother, Semira doesn’t like reading novels and poems.’

options.A: Semira doesn’t like her elder brother.
options.B: Semira doesn’t like reading novels and poems but her brother does.
options.C: Semira likes her elder brother, but he doesn’t.
options.D: Semira and her elder brother do not like reading.
options.E: Semira and her elder brother do not like each other.

explanation_steps: ‘Unlike her brother’ = her brother is different: he DOES like reading novels and poems; Semira doesn’t.
Answer: B.
tips: unlike X = X is different in this respect.

similar_questions.stem: ‘Unlike his father, Tesfay drinks coffee.’

options.A: Tesfay and his father drink coffee.
options.B: Tesfay drinks coffee but his father doesn’t.

explanation_steps: The father is different. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘It is unlikely that the price of oil will go up.’

options.A: The price of oil is not expected to increase.
options.B: The price of oil is expected to increase.
options.C: The price of oil is not expected to decrease.
options.D: People would like the price of oil to increase.
options.E: The price of oil is likely to decrease.

explanation_steps: unlikely = probably will not happen; go up = increase.
So an increase is not expected. E says more (a decrease is likely), which is not stated. Answer: A.
tips: Do not add information: ‘not going up’ ≠ ‘going down’.

similar_questions.stem: ‘It is unlikely that it will rain today.’

options.C: It will be sunny for sure.

explanation_steps: unlikely = not expected. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘Contrary to everybody’s expectation it rained.’

options.A: Very few people expected that it would rain.
options.B: Very few people expected that it would not rain.
options.C: Everyone expected that it would rain.
options.D: No one expected that it would rain.
options.E: No one expected that it would not rain.

explanation_steps: contrary to everybody’s expectation = the opposite of what everybody expected.
It rained, so everybody expected no rain → No one expected that it would rain. Answer: D.
tips: ‘everybody’ in the original matches ‘no one’ (not ‘very few’) in the paraphrase.

similar_questions.stem: ‘Contrary to all expectations, our team won.’

options.C: A few people expected us to lose.

explanation_steps: Opposite of expectation. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Choose the alternative that best represents the italicized sentence: ‘The student would have stood first if the 10 points had been added.’

options.A: The student stood first since the 10 points were added.
options.B: The student did not stand first although the 10 points were added.
options.C: The 10 points were added but the student stood second.
options.D: The student did not want the 10 points to be added.
options.E: The 10 points were not added, so the student did not stand first.

explanation_steps: Third conditional (would have + pp … if + had been) = an unreal past: the opposite of both clauses is true.
The points were NOT added and the student did NOT stand first. Answer: E.
tips: Third conditional → reverse both clauses to find the facts.

similar_questions.stem: ‘If he had left earlier, he would have caught the bus.’

options.A: He left early and caught the bus.
options.B: He didn’t leave early, so he missed the bus.
options.C: He left early but missed the bus.
options.D: He caught the bus although he was late.

explanation_steps: Reverse both clauses. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.rule: If + had + pp, would have + pp = neither happened.

questions.stem:
PART II: PARAGRAPH WRITING. Write a meaningful and grammatically correct paragraph of about 200 words on ONE of the topics provided. You are advised to spend ONE HOUR writing your paragraph. During this time, you should prepare an outline, write and make any necessary changes to your paragraph. Write the final copy of your paragraph on the answer sheet provided; you may use the space marked ‘ROUGH WORK’ to outline your paragraph. Check and revise your paragraph. Your paragraph will be graded on Content, Language, and Organization.
Topics to choose from:
1. Write about how climate change may affect the lives of people in the world.
2. Describe your daily activities at your school to a friend who lives outside the country.
questions.answer:
Write ONE paragraph on ONE topic.

Model paragraph for Topic 1 (197 words):
Climate change may affect the lives of people all over the world in several serious ways. First of all, rising temperatures will make droughts longer and more frequent in many regions, including the Horn of Africa. When the rains fail, crops dry up and animals die, so farmers lose their income and food becomes scarce and expensive. Secondly, in other parts of the world the opposite problem will occur: heavier storms and floods will destroy houses, roads and farmland. In addition, as the ice at the poles melts, the level of the sea will rise, and people living on low coasts and small islands may be forced to leave their homes. Moreover, climate change can harm people’s health. Hot weather spreads diseases such as malaria to new areas, and heat waves are dangerous for old people and young children. Finally, shortages of water and land may cause conflicts and push millions of people to migrate to cities or to other countries. In conclusion, climate change is not only an environmental problem but also a threat to food, homes, health and peace, so every country and every person should act now to reduce pollution and plant more trees.

Model paragraph for Topic 2 (201 words):
Dear Sara, you asked me what a normal school day is like for me in Eritrea, so let me describe it. I wake up at six o’clock every morning, wash, have a quick breakfast of bread and tea, and walk to school with my friends. Lessons begin at a quarter to eight, after the flag ceremony in the school compound. In the morning we usually have four periods of forty minutes each, for example mathematics, English, biology and chemistry. At ten o’clock there is a short break, when we chat, play volleyball or buy snacks from the school shop. After the break we have three more periods, and at lunchtime I go home to eat with my family. In the afternoon I sometimes return to school for tutorial classes or club activities; I am a member of the green club, so we water the trees and plant new seedlings. In the evening I help my mother at home, and then I study for about three hours, because we are preparing for the national examination this year. Finally, I go to bed at about ten o’clock, tired but happy. I would love to hear how your school day is different from mine.

Plan: topic sentence (main idea) → 3–4 supporting points with examples → concluding sentence.
Topic 1 linkers: first of all, secondly, in addition, moreover, as a result, so, finally. Topic 2 linkers: first, then, after that, at ten o’clock, in the afternoon, in the evening, finally.

marking_points: Content (8): relevant topic sentence and 3–4 developed supporting points; comparison topics must compare (similarities and differences), not just describe.
Organization (6): topic sentence, logically ordered supporting sentences with transitions, a concluding sentence; ONE paragraph; unity (no irrelevant sentences).
Language (6): grammar (tenses, agreement, articles, comparatives), vocabulary, spelling and punctuation.
Length: about 200 words; clearly shorter paragraphs lose content marks.

descriptors: 7–8: clear topic sentence; 3–4 well-developed, relevant supporting points with examples or explanations; for comparison topics real similarities AND differences; about 200 words.
5–6: relevant with some support, but one point is thin or repeated.
3–4: few ideas, little support, partly off topic, or clearly too short (under about 120 words).
5–6: topic sentence → ordered supporting sentences → concluding sentence; one main idea only; smooth transitions (first of all, moreover, however, whereas, in conclusion).
3–4: logical overall, but weak or missing concluding sentence, few or repeated linkers, or one sentence off the main idea.
1–2: ideas in random order; no clear topic sentence; written as a list or several paragraphs.
5–6: accurate tenses, agreement and articles; varied sentence types; suitable vocabulary (comparatives and contrast words for comparison topics); correct spelling, capitals and punctuation.
3–4: several errors that do not block meaning; limited sentence variety or vocabulary.
1–2: frequent errors that sometimes block meaning.
0: errors make the paragraph impossible to follow.

planning_template: Topic chosen: ______ (write about ONE topic only; one paragraph of about 200 words).
Supporting point 1 + example/explanation (Topic 1: drought and food / Topic 2: morning lessons): ______
Supporting point 2 + example/explanation (Topic 1: floods and sea level / Topic 2: break-time activities): ______
Supporting point 3 + example/explanation (Topic 1: health / Topic 2: afternoon clubs and tutorials): ______
Supporting point 4 + example/explanation (Topic 1: conflict and migration / Topic 2: evening study): ______
Linking words to use: first of all, secondly, moreover, in addition, however, on the other hand, whereas, while, finally
Concluding sentence (restate the main idea / give a final comparison or advice): ______
Check (5 minutes): one paragraph, first line indented; tenses, agreement, articles, spelling, capital letters, full stops; about 200 words.
tips: Topic 1 asks for effects on PEOPLE’S LIVES – explain how each change (drought, floods, sea level, disease) affects food, homes, health or work, rather than only describing the weather.
Topic 2 asks for DAILY activities AT SCHOOL – keep home activities short and do not turn it into a full letter with addresses; one paragraph is required.

similar_questions.stem: Write a paragraph of about 200 words on how the mobile phone has changed the lives of young people.
similar_questions.answer: Model: The mobile phone has changed the lives of young people in many ways. First of all, it has made communication fast and cheap: students can call or text their families and friends at any time, even when they live far away. Secondly, it has become an important tool for learning. With internet access, young people can look up information, watch educational videos and share notes with classmates. In addition, the phone has changed the way young people spend their free time, because many of them now play games, listen to music and follow social media for hours every day. However, not all the effects are positive. Too much time on the phone can reduce sleep, distract students from their studies and weaken face-to-face friendships. Moreover, some young people spend money on airtime that their families need for other things. In conclusion, the mobile phone is a powerful tool that can improve young people’s lives if they use it wisely, but it can also harm their studies and health if they cannot control how much they use it.
explanation_steps: Topic sentence states the main idea (many changes).
Each supporting sentence gives one effect with an example, joined by linkers.
The concluding sentence gives a balanced judgement.
